ConocoPhillips fell 3.3% today to $127.53, continuing a sharp six-day decline that has wiped out 6.6% of the stock's value since mid-September. The selloff tracks a collapse in U.S. oil prices—crude tumbled from $107 to below $100 per barrel this week as traders bet that escalating U.S.-Iran tensions might actually lead to talks rather than conflict, reducing the threat of supply disruptions. Even as Middle East instability persists (Iranian airliners face shutdown, the Strait of Hormuz remains closed, Saudi pipeline constraints tighten Asian supply), the market's focus has shifted from "war premium" to de-escalation hopes, leaving oil prices lower and energy stocks weaker.

The divergence between U.S. crude ($107) and world oil ($130.80) suggests traders still see regional supply tightness, but that hasn't been enough to hold up COP's stock. For an oil producer, lower crude prices directly compress margins and cash flow, and the absence of a geopolitical "shock premium" removes one of the few near-term catalysts that could offset the macro headwind.
